paragraphs.title: The Vision of the End and Destruction

easy.explanation: The LORD showed Amos a basket of summer fruit.
easy.q: What did the LORD show Amos in the vision?

easy.explanation: The LORD said, “The end is come upon my people of Israel.”
easy.q: What did the LORD say had come upon Israel?

answers: They would become louder songs of joy
They would be sung in another land
easy.explanation: The songs of the temple would become howlings in that day.
easy.q: What would happen to the songs of the temple?

answers: The end that had come upon Israel
medium.explanation: The vision signified that the end had come upon Israel.
medium.q: What did the basket of summer fruit represent?

medium.explanation: The passage says there would be many dead bodies in every place.
medium.q: According to the passage, what would be found in every place?

answers: From temple songs to cries of grief and death
medium.explanation: Temple songs would become howlings, and the land would be filled with dead bodies.
medium.q: What change in atmosphere is described?

answers: Joy will be replaced by mourning
The singers will learn new instruments
challenge.explanation: The change shows that worshipful celebration will be replaced by grief.
challenge.q: What does the change from songs to howlings suggest?

answers: Many dead bodies in every place
Amos being asked what he saw
challenge.explanation: The phrase “many dead bodies in every place” portrays widespread destruction.
challenge.q: Which detail most strongly emphasizes the severity of the judgment?

challenge.explanation: The statement announces the coming end and judgment of Israel.
challenge.q: In context, what does “The end is come” mean?

paragraphs.title: The Exploitation of the Poor in Trade

answers: Those who swallow up the needy
Those who sing in the temple
easy.explanation: The prophet addresses those who swallow up the needy and make the poor fail.

answers: The new moon and the sabbath to be over
The beginning of a new harvest
easy.explanation: They asked when the new moon and sabbath would be gone so they could resume selling.
easy.q: What were the dishonest merchants waiting for?

easy.explanation: They planned to sell the refuse, or waste, of the wheat.
easy.q: What did they intend to sell with the wheat?

answers: By using false measures and balances
By giving extra grain to the poor
medium.explanation: They made the ephah small, the shekel great, and falsified the balances by deceit.
medium.q: How did the merchants deceive people?

medium.explanation: An ephah was a measure for grain and other dry goods.
medium.q: In this passage, what is an “ephah”?

answers: Buy them for silver and for a pair of shoes
medium.explanation: They wanted to buy the poor for silver and the needy for a pair of shoes.
medium.q: What did the merchants hope to do to the poor and needy?

answers: They wanted to resume their dishonest trade
They wanted to observe the days more carefully
They wanted to stop selling to the poor
challenge.explanation: They viewed the sacred days as an interruption to their deceptive business.
challenge.q: Why were the merchants eager for the new moon and sabbath to end?

answers: He will never forget their works
challenge.explanation: The LORD swears, “Surely I will never forget any of their works.”
challenge.q: What does the LORD's oath in verse 7 reveal?

answers: They combine oppression of the poor with dishonest trade
They sell large amounts of grain
challenge.explanation: They exploit needy people while manipulating measures, weights, and balances.
challenge.q: Why are the merchants' actions especially serious?

paragraphs.title: The Trembling Land and National Mourning

easy.explanation: The passage asks whether the land would not tremble because of these things.
easy.q: What would happen to the land because of these sins?

answers: It would go down at noon
easy.explanation: The LORD said He would cause the sun to go down at noon.
easy.q: What would happen to the sun?

easy.explanation: The LORD would turn their feasts into mourning.

answers: It would affect only one city
The whole land and its inhabitants would be affected
medium.explanation: The land would tremble and everyone who dwelt there would mourn.
medium.q: How extensive would the disaster be?

answers: It would rise and be cast out like the flood of Egypt
It would bloom like a garden
It would become a fortified city
medium.explanation: The land is compared to something overwhelmed, cast out, and drowned by the flood of Egypt.
medium.q: What image is used to describe the land's destruction?

answers: Both express a change from joy to darkness and grief
medium.explanation: The signs together portray national judgment and the loss of celebration.
medium.q: What do the darkened sun and mourning feasts have in common?

answers: Expressions of joy become expressions of grief
The number of feasts will increase
challenge.explanation: The songs will no longer celebrate; they will express sorrow.
challenge.q: What is the significance of turning songs into lamentation?

answers: The trembling land and the mourning of its inhabitants
The temple songs and the summer fruit
The new moon and the sabbath
challenge.explanation: The trembling land represents physical upheaval, while mourning represents human suffering.
challenge.q: Which pair shows both damage to creation and suffering among people?

challenge.explanation: The comparison conveys especially deep and painful mourning.
challenge.q: What does the mourning of “an only son” emphasize?

paragraphs.title: The Famine for Hearing God's Word

answers: A famine of hearing the words of the LORD
easy.explanation: The passage describes a famine not of bread, but of hearing the words of the LORD.
easy.q: What kind of famine would come upon the land?

easy.explanation: They would wander from sea to sea and run to and fro to seek the word of the LORD.
easy.q: What would people do while seeking the word of the LORD?

answers: They would find the word of the LORD
They would fall and never rise again
easy.explanation: The passage says they would fall and never rise up again.
easy.q: What would happen to those who swore by the false worship centers?

answers: It is a famine of bread and water
It is a famine of hearing God's word
It is a famine of grain only
medium.explanation: The passage explicitly says it is not a famine of bread or a thirst for water.
medium.q: How is this famine different from an ordinary famine?

answers: Move from place to place in search of something
medium.explanation: The people travel from place to place looking for the word of the LORD.
medium.q: What does “wander” mean in this context?

answers: No, they would not find it
They would stop seeking before they left
medium.explanation: They would run to and fro to seek the word of the LORD, but would not find it.
medium.q: Would the people find what they were seeking?

answers: The absence of God's word produces desperate searching
The wandering is for buying grain
The wandering is part of a joyful feast
challenge.explanation: Because they cannot hear God's word, they search throughout the land without finding it.
challenge.q: What is the relationship between the spiritual famine and the people's wandering?

answers: A severe condition affecting the whole community
challenge.explanation: These images together describe widespread weakness and distress.
challenge.q: What does the combination of famine, thirst, and fainting suggest?

answers: They are connected with the people's false oaths and worship
They formed a successful trade route
They were places where God's word would certainly be found
challenge.explanation: The locations are named in connection with oaths to false religious powers and the resulting judgment.
challenge.q: Why are Samaria, Dan, and Beer-sheba mentioned?
